blocks.text: **The task.** An array of heights forms an elevation map, each bar 1 unit wide. Compute how much rainwater is trapped between the bars after it rains.
Do not think about pools. Think about **one column at a time**.

How much water sits above position `i`? It is held in by the tallest bar somewhere to its left and the tallest somewhere to its right. Water rises to the lower of those two, minus the bar already there:

blocks.code: water at i  =  min(maxLeft, maxRight)  -  height[i]

blocks.text: Apply that to every position and sum. The only question left is how to know both maxima cheaply.
Precompute two arrays — running maximum from the left, running maximum from the right — then sweep once. That is O(N) time but **O(N) space**.
We can drop the arrays entirely. Walk from both ends, tracking the best height seen so far on each side.

Here is the crucial observation: if `maxLeft < maxRight`, then the water at the left position is decided by `maxLeft` **regardless of what lies between**. Some bar on the right is already known to be at least `maxRight`, which is taller — so the left side is the binding constraint, and we can commit to it safely.

We always process the **shorter** side. That guarantees the taller side acts as a wall we have already confirmed exists, so the running maximum on the short side is the true limit for that column. No lookahead required.
It is the same reasoning as the container problem: process the binding constraint, trust the other side.
**Time: O(N)** — one pass. **Space: O(1)** — four numbers, no arrays.
This problem is a classic interview question precisely because the O(N)/O(1) solution requires the per-column reframing. If you find it hard, that is expected — it rewards rereading.
